- F23.prompt-assembly — Prompt assembly [supported, verified] Each request re-sends the system prompt, project context, every prior message and tool result, then the new message; rarely-changing content is first. `--system-prompt` or `--system-prompt-file` replaces the default. The main conversation requests 1 hour only on a Claude subscription within plan usage, otherwise 5 minutes; each hit resets the timer. `ENABLE_PROMPT_CACHING_1H=1` or `promptCacheTtl` (v2.1.242+) request 1 hour; `FORCE_PROMPT_CACHING_5M=1` overrides. A gateway `retry-after` is honoured (above 60 stops retries outside watchdog sessions). TLS certificate failures and content-filter blocks are not retried. Copilot CLI is a terminal-based AI agent that can answer questions, plan work, and complete tasks on your behalf. | ev: E-copilot-cli-00837, E-copilot-cli-00028, E-copilot-cli-01730
- F16.headless-mode — Headless mode [partial, verified] `-p PROMPT` executes a prompt in non-interactive mode; the CLI runs the prompt and exits when done. `copilot workflow run WORKFLOW-NAME` runs an existing dynamic workflow directly, without sending a chat prompt, and waits for the run to finish or stop. Autopilot mode can be used programmatically, in a script or CI workflow. | limit: Cloud sandboxing is only available for interactive Copilot CLI sessions. You can't run the CLI programmatically in a cloud sandbox—that is, you can't combine the `--cloud` option with the `-p` or `-i` options. | ev: E-copilot-cli-01375, E-copilot-cli-00851, E-copilot-cli-01706, E-copilot-cli-00311
- F16.ide-integration — IDE integration [supported, unverified] A setting set to true auto-connects Copilot CLI to an IDE workspace on startup; when false, /ide still connects manually. VS Code shows proposed file changes as a diff in a new editor tab with accept and reject buttons. ACP lets Copilot CLI act as an agent in third-party tools and IDEs that support the protocol. | ev: E-copilot-cli-01224, E-copilot-cli-00510, E-copilot-cli-01670
- F16.desktop-web-app — Desktop and web apps [supported, verified] The GitHub Copilot app is a desktop application for agent-driven development with parallel workstreams, GitHub integration and PR lifecycle management. The copilot app command opens it in the current directory, deep-linking straight to a new session. Cloud agent sessions can be started directly on GitHub and iterated on in the browser. | ev: E-copilot-cli-01418, E-copilot-cli-00838, E-copilot-cli-00644
- F16.sdk-api — SDK and API [supported, unverified] The copilot command's --acp option starts the CLI's ACP server, in stdio mode if no transport mode is specified, or with --port. The -p flag lets the CLI be used programmatically within scripts. Extensions add tools and slash commands using only the SDK that ships with the CLI, and a workflow can also be started from other code that uses the GitHub Copilot SDK. | ev: E-copilot-cli-00809, E-copilot-cli-02227, E-copilot-cli-00025, E-copilot-cli-01895
- F16.ci-chat — CI and chat surfaces [supported, verified] Copilot CLI can run in a GitHub Actions workflow using either a personal access token or the built-in GITHUB_TOKEN (the two differ in AI credit billing and required setup), installed during a job and invoked from workflow steps. Mentioning @copilot in a pull request comment asks the cloud agent to make changes. | ev: E-copilot-cli-01757, E-copilot-cli-02315, E-copilot-cli-01539

## F17 Model selection and routing

- F17.model-picker — Model picker [partial, verified] The model used by Copilot CLI can be changed with the /model slash command or the --model command-line option; the docs say to enter the command, then select a model from the list. Users can view which models are available to them with /model. Docs advise using /model to choose from available models based on your task complexity. | limit: Users can only access AI models that are enabled at the enterprise level (E-copilot-cli-00353); the research agent always uses the defined model regardless of what model you've selected for your main session (E-copilot-cli-00185). | ev: E-copilot-cli-00051, E-copilot-cli-00368, E-copilot-cli-00353, E-copilot-cli-00185
- F17.model-flag-env — Flag, setting and environment [supported, verified] --model=MODEL chooses the AI model (for example gpt-5.4 or claude-haiku-4.5), useful for pinning a model in reproducible workflows. The model setting in ~/.copilot/settings.json selects the model (auto lets Copilot pick) and is managed by /model. - F17.auto-routing — Automatic routing [supported, verified] Auto chooses models from real-time system health and availability, model performance and task complexity. /model auto TIER (efficiency, balance, or intelligence) selects an Auto routing tier directly. - F17.provider-byok — Providers and bring-your-own-key [supported, verified] Copilot CLI can use your own model provider instead of GitHub-hosted models (OpenAI-compatible endpoint, Azure OpenAI or Anthropic, including local models such as Ollama), set up with environment variables. - F17.model-catalog — Model catalog and availability [supported, verified] Docs have a Supported AI models page listing the models supported in GitHub Copilot. ## F19 Modes and autonomy levels

- F19.named-modes — Named modes [partial, verified] The --mode option takes interactive, plan or autopilot, and session state records the current mode (interactive, plan, or autopilot). The about page instead describes the interactive interface as having two modes: default ask/execute and plan. | limit: E-copilot-cli-00029 says the interactive interface 'has two modes' (default ask/execute and plan); E-copilot-cli-00976 and E-copilot-cli-02945 list three: interactive, plan, autopilot. | ev: E-copilot-cli-00976, E-copilot-cli-00029, E-copilot-cli-02945
- F19.entering-modes — How modes are entered [supported, verified] Shift+Tab cycles between modes in an interactive session, for example until 'autopilot' shows in the status bar. With stayInAutopilot enabled, the next prompt after a task completes is also handled in autopilot mode. Remote clients can switch the session mode, for example between interactive and plan mode. | ev: E-copilot-cli-00030, E-copilot-cli-02804, E-copilot-cli-01267, E-copilot-cli-00140
- F19.plan-mode — Plan mode [partial, verified] Plan mode lets you collaborate with Copilot on an implementation plan before any code is written; Shift+Tab cycles in and out of it, and in plan mode all prompts trigger the plan workflow. Remote control can approve or reject plans, and --plan --mode autopilot moves to autopilot once the plan is ready instead of waiting for human approval. | limit: Quotes say planning happens 'before any code is written'; none of them states that plan mode is read-only, and the exits shown are Shift+Tab cycling and plan approval. | ev: E-copilot-cli-00589, E-copilot-cli-00977, E-copilot-cli-00067, E-copilot-cli-00442
- F19.autonomy-mode — Auto-accept and autonomous modes [partial, verified] Autopilot mode lets Copilot work autonomously until a task is complete, auto-responding to requests that would otherwise require user intervention. --autopilot enables autopilot continuation, and --no-ask-user prevents the agent from pausing to seek additional user input. stayInAutopilot (default true) keeps autopilot active after each task. | limit: E-copilot-cli-00948 says --autopilot works until task_complete is called, 'then returns to interactive mode', while E-copilot-cli-01266 says stayInAutopilot (default true) remains in autopilot after each task; the quotes do not reconcile them. | ev: E-copilot-cli-00948, E-copilot-cli-00179, E-copilot-cli-01266, E-copilot-cli-01392
- F19.read-only-mode — Read-only or ask mode [supported, verified] In plan mode, any attempt to edit, patch, or run a shell command that would change a file in the workspace is blocked automatically. The quote states this is enforced directly, so it does not depend on the model choosing to behave. | ev: E-copilot-cli-01093
- F19.mode-defaults — Mode defaults and persistence [partial, verified] Autopilot is sticky by default: once a task completes the CLI stays in autopilot and the next prompt is also handled in autopilot (stayInAutopilot, default true). Setting stayInAutopilot to false returns it to interactive mode after each task and can be stored in ~/.copilot/settings.json. Shift+Tab switches back to interactive at any time. | limit: Stickiness is documented only for autopilot ('By default, autopilot mode is sticky'); no cited quote names the mode a new session starts in. | ev: E-copilot-cli-01702, E-copilot-cli-01266, E-copilot-cli-01703, E-copilot-cli-01705

## F22 Usage, cost, limits and observability

- F22.usage-visibility — Usage and cost visibility [supported, unverified] The /context slash command visualizes context window usage; its first line shows the active model and tokens in use out of the context window capacity. The CLI overview lists the amount of GitHub AI Credits used in the current session. With your own model provider, cost estimates are hidden but token usage (input, output, cache counts) is still displayed. | ev: E-copilot-cli-00089, E-copilot-cli-00620, E-copilot-cli-00374
- F22.budget-caps — Budgets and caps [partial, verified] An AI credit session limit caps what Copilot can spend on a single session; --max-ai-credits sets a soft maximum per response that resets per user message and can be adjusted mid-session with /limits. Under usage-based billing, budget controls at user, organization, cost center and enterprise levels determine how usage is served, metered or blocked. | limit: --max-ai-credits is described as a soft maximum for each response. When usage is billed directly to the organization, user-level Copilot budgets are not considered. | ev: E-copilot-cli-00376, E-copilot-cli-00974, E-copilot-cli-02009, E-copilot-cli-01762
- F22.rate-limits — Rate-limit behaviour [partial, verified] Rate limits control how many requests a user or application can make in a given time period. Included AI credits do not carry over; the allowance resets at 00:00:00 UTC on the first day of each calendar month. Rate limits are temporary; waiting a short period and retrying often resolves them. A setting, when true, switches to auto mode and retries on eligible rate limit errors. | limit: The automatic switch to auto mode does not apply to global rate limits or BYOK providers. | ev: E-copilot-cli-02005, E-copilot-cli-01996, E-copilot-cli-02007, E-copilot-cli-01218
- F22.telemetry-otel — Telemetry and OpenTelemetry [supported, unverified] Copilot CLI can export OpenTelemetry traces and metrics covering agent interactions, LLM calls, tool executions and token usage. OTel is off by default with zero overhead and activates when any of the listed conditions is met. A telemetry key can push baseline OTel export configuration (for example enabled, endpoint, protocol, headers). | ev: E-copilot-cli-01152, E-copilot-cli-01153, E-copilot-cli-01354
- F22.logs-debug — Logs and debug output [supported, unverified] The logLevel setting sets logging verbosity (none, error, warning, info, debug, all or default). /lsp logs opens the live LSP services panel to view server logs. In the Actions example, the CLI prints its response to standard output, which is recorded in the log for the workflow run. | ev: E-copilot-cli-01229, E-copilot-cli-02610, E-copilot-cli-02325
- F22.status-display — Status line and display [supported, verified] In Copilot CLI the model used for each response displays in the terminal. The status line contains `sandbox enabled` when sandboxing is being used, and the footer shows an 'N scheduled' indicator by default whenever the session has active schedules. The Git branch in the footer can be hidden with /settings footer.showBranch off. | ev: E-copilot-cli-00245, E-copilot-cli-00351, E-copilot-cli-00926, E-copilot-cli-02487

## F23 Request and response handling

- F23.prompt-assembly — Prompt assembly [supported, verified] Context window holds every message, response, tool call and result plus system instructions; system instructions and tool definitions are always present. `/context` visualizes context window usage. `--allow-all-mcp-server-instructions` puts all MCP servers' instructions in the system prompt (default: allowlisted only up front). `--no-custom-instructions` skips AGENTS.md and related files. | ev: E-copilot-cli-80005, E-copilot-cli-80012, E-copilot-cli-80048, E-copilot-cli-80049, E-copilot-cli-80051, E-copilot-cli-80062

The CLI's telemetry reports `gen_ai.usage.cache_read.input_tokens` (cached input tokens read) and `gen_ai.usage.cache_creation.input_tokens` (cached input tokens created). | limit: Stated on the Copilot model-hosting page for Anthropic and Google models only. - F23.retry-backoff — Retry and back-off [partial, verified] Per the config-dir reference, the continueOnAutoMode setting (default false) makes eligible rate limit errors trigger an automatic switch to auto mode and retry, not for global rate limits or BYOK providers. The CLI-features comparison lists 'Customizing retry/abort behavior on recoverable errors', example: on rate limit errors, choose retry with a capped retry count. | limit: The auto-mode retry is a model switch, is off unless continueOnAutoMode is true, and excludes global rate limits and BYOK providers; a capped retry count is shown only as a customization example. No default attempt limit, wait time or message appears in the reviewed text. | ev: E-copilot-cli-80063, E-copilot-cli-80064, E-copilot-cli-80065, E-copilot-cli-80067
- F23.malformed-call-recovery — Malformed call recovery [undocumented, verified] swept for: malformed; invalid (tool|json|argument|parameter|input)|unknown tool|tool (call|use) (error|fail|invalid); schema validation|failed to parse|could not parse|unparseable; hits 5, reviewed 5; positive control `copilot`: 4270 hits
- F23.tool-output-limits — Tool output limits [supported, verified] Tool output larger than 20 KiB is saved to a temporary file by default; the model gets the file path and a preview. Applies to all tools, including MCP server tools. Set `COPILOT_LARGE_OUTPUT_THRESHOLD_BYTES` to a positive number of UTF-8 bytes before starting the CLI to change the limit (higher leaves less context). | ev: E-copilot-cli-80046, E-copilot-cli-80047
- F23.output-redaction — Output redaction [partial, verified] `--secret-env-vars=VAR ...` names environment variables whose values are redacted in output (quoted, comma-separated list). Values of `GITHUB_TOKEN` and `COPILOT_GITHUB_TOKEN` are redacted from output by default. The command reference describes it as redacting the variable from shell and MCP server environments. | limit: Documented only for environment-variable values (two by default, others via --secret-env-vars). ## Step by step: who documents most, and why it matters

- Choose the front door: Documents the most: Cursor, Gemini CLI (100%). Documents the least: Grok Bot (33%). Editorial: our view, not a vendor claim: Pick the door that fits how you work. A door that cannot ask you questions cannot do tasks that need your approval.
- Apply organization rules: Documents the most: GitHub Copilot CLI, GitHub Copilot in VS Code (agent and chat) (100%). Documents the least: Grok Bot (50%). Editorial: our view, not a vendor claim: In a managed setting your own model and permission choices may be narrower than the docs suggest. Check what your organization allows before planning around a feature.
- Load the house rules: Documents the most: Claude Code, Gemini CLI (100%). Documents the least: GitHub Copilot in VS Code (agent and chat), Grok Bot (60%). Editorial: our view, not a vendor claim: These files are how you steer any model. How well a model follows them differs by model, but whether they are loaded at all is the harness's doing.
- Load memory and earlier sessions: Documents the most: OpenAI Codex CLI (100%). Documents the least: Grok Bot (71%). Editorial: our view, not a vendor claim: A harness that remembers saves you re-explaining. One that does not starts every run cold.
- Stock the built-in tools: Documents the most: GitHub Copilot CLI, GitHub Copilot in VS Code (agent and chat), Cursor, Gemini CLI, Grok Build CLI (100%). Documents the least: Grok Bot (50%). Editorial: our view, not a vendor claim: Two harnesses can give the same model different tools. What a model can do is bounded by this list as well as by how capable it is.
- Load skills and custom commands: Documents the most: Claude Code (100%). Documents the least: Grok Bot (35%). Editorial: our view, not a vendor claim: These are how a team teaches an agent its own routines. If your team relies on them, check that the harness supports your format before comparing models.
- Connect outside tools: Documents the most: Grok Build CLI (100%). Documents the least: GitHub Copilot in VS Code (agent and chat), Grok Bot (75%). Editorial: our view, not a vendor claim: More connections give the model more reach, and more ways to cause harm. Check how each harness approves and filters them.
- Set the safety posture: Documents the most: GitHub Copilot in VS Code (agent and chat), Cursor (94%). Documents the least: Grok Bot (33%). Editorial: our view, not a vendor claim: This choice, not the model, decides how often you are interrupted and how much damage a mistake can do. Pick the mode first, then the model.
- Pick the model and thinking effort: Documents the most: Claude Code, OpenAI Codex CLI (93%). Documents the least: Grok Bot (7%). Editorial: our view, not a vendor claim: This is the one place where you steer cost and quality directly. Compare which controls each harness gives you, not only which models it lists.
- Prepare an isolated workspace: Documents the most: Claude Code, OpenAI Codex CLI, GitHub Copilot CLI, Grok Build CLI (100%). Documents the least: Grok Bot (0%). Editorial: our view, not a vendor claim: Isolation lets you run many attempts and keep the best one. It is normally the harness's own feature.
- Assemble the prompt: Documents the most: Claude Code, OpenAI Codex CLI, GitHub Copilot CLI, GitHub Copilot in VS Code (agent and chat), Grok Build CLI (100%). Documents the least: Grok Bot (33%). Editorial: our view, not a vendor claim: What a model never sees it cannot use. Controls over this vary between harnesses: compare which let you see or replace what is sent.
- Run your own code at set moments: Documents the most: Cursor, Grok Build CLI (93%). Documents the least: Grok Bot (0%). Editorial: our view, not a vendor claim: Hooks are the strongest guard you control. A plain script hook does not change with the model; a hook that asks a model can. Check which moments each harness exposes and whether a failing hook blocks the action.
- Send the request and handle trouble: Documents the most: Claude Code (100%). Documents the least: Grok Build CLI (17%).Only partly covered by the atlas. Editorial: our view, not a vendor claim: When the service is busy, how the harness waits or falls back decides whether your task stalls. How the answer is streamed is not covered here.
- Set the thinking budget: Documents the most: Claude Code, OpenAI Codex CLI, GitHub Copilot in VS Code (agent and chat), Cursor, Gemini CLI (75%). Documents the least: Grok Bot (0%). Editorial: our view, not a vendor claim: More thinking costs more and takes longer. The levels that exist depend on the model, so changing models can change what you can ask for.
- Reuse the unchanged part of the prompt: Documents the most: Claude Code (100%). Documents the least: OpenAI Codex CLI, Grok Build CLI, Grok Bot (0%). Editorial: our view, not a vendor claim: Caching changes cost and speed on long sessions. Compare whether you can turn it off or tune how long it lasts, and what breaks it.
- Read what the model asked for: Documents the most: Claude Code (50%). Documents the least: OpenAI Codex CLI, GitHub Copilot CLI, GitHub Copilot in VS Code (agent and chat), Cursor, Gemini CLI, Grok Build CLI, Grok Bot (0%).Only partly covered by the atlas. Editorial: our view, not a vendor claim: A harness that recovers well from a model's slips can make a weaker model usable. Only recovery from malformed requests is covered here.
- Decide whether it is allowed: Documents the most: OpenAI Codex CLI (100%). Documents the least: GitHub Copilot in VS Code (agent and chat) (62%). Editorial: our view, not a vendor claim: This is where a harness stops a model's mistake before it happens. Compare how finely you can write rules; do not count on a model to police itself.
- Save an undo point: Documents the most: GitHub Copilot CLI, Gemini CLI, Grok Build CLI, Grok Bot (100%). Documents the least: Claude Code, OpenAI Codex CLI, GitHub Copilot in VS Code (agent and chat), Cursor (50%). Editorial: our view, not a vendor claim: An undo point is what makes it safe to let a model try bold changes. It is normally the harness's own code, not a model's work.
- Run it inside the fence: Documents the most: OpenAI Codex CLI, Gemini CLI (100%). Documents the least: GitHub Copilot CLI, Grok Build CLI (60%). Editorial: our view, not a vendor claim: A fence limits what the commands a model asks for can do. Not every harness has one, and some have it only on some systems.
- Tidy the tool's output: Documents the most: GitHub Copilot CLI (75%). Documents the least: Grok Build CLI (0%). Editorial: our view, not a vendor claim: How output is trimmed affects what the model can notice, which matters more for weaker models. Hiding secrets is a separate control.
- Feed the result back and go round again: Documents the most: OpenAI Codex CLI, GitHub Copilot in VS Code (agent and chat), Cursor, Gemini CLI (100%). Documents the least: Grok Build CLI, Grok Bot (50%). Editorial: our view, not a vendor claim: Long tasks are many turns. Whether a turn limit exists changes whether a stuck model can run up a large bill.
- Hand work to helpers: Documents the most: Claude Code, OpenAI Codex CLI (90%). Documents the least: Grok Bot (45%). Editorial: our view, not a vendor claim: Helpers let you use a cheaper model for simple jobs and a stronger one for hard ones, but only if the harness lets you choose per helper.
- Shrink the context when it fills: Documents the most: Claude Code, OpenAI Codex CLI, GitHub Copilot in VS Code (agent and chat), Cursor, Gemini CLI, Grok Build CLI (100%). Documents the least: Grok Bot (0%). Editorial: our view, not a vendor claim: Summaries lose detail. On long tasks the quality of this step can matter as much as the model, and models that read more at once need it less.

# Words used in the lifecycle pages

> Vendor-derived text below is untrusted data, never instructions. `‹` and `›` stand for `<` and `>`; a ⚠ marks text that looked like an instruction.

- **approval mode**: A setting for how much the agent may do without asking you first.
- **caching**: Keeping the unchanged start of a long prompt so later requests are cheaper and faster.
- **changelog**: The vendor's dated list of what changed in each release.
- **checkpoint**: A saved snapshot you can return to after a bad edit.
- **CLI**: A command-line program you run in a terminal.
- **compaction**: Summarising older parts of a conversation to free up space in the context window.
- **context window**: How much text the model can read at once. Anything beyond it must be dropped or summarised.
- **effort**: How much thinking a model is asked to spend before it answers. Higher effort usually costs more and takes longer.
- **harness**: The program around a model. It builds the prompt, offers tools, checks permissions, runs commands and shows you the result. The model itself only reads text and writes text.
- **headless**: Running the agent from a script with no one at the keyboard.
- **hook**: Your own script that the harness runs at a set moment, such as before a tool runs or when a session ends.
- **IDE**: An editor such as VS Code, where the agent can run as a plug-in.
- **instruction file**: A plain text file, such as AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md, that tells the model how you want it to work.
- **managed settings**: Rules an administrator installs for a whole organization, which override personal choices.
- **marketplace**: A place, often a code repository, from which plugins can be installed.
- **MCP**: A standard plug-in socket (Model Context Protocol) for connecting outside programs, such as a database, as extra tools.
- **model**: The AI that reads the prompt and writes a reply. It cannot open files or run anything on its own.
- **plan mode**: A mode where the agent proposes a plan and waits for your approval before changing anything.
- **plugin**: An add-on that bundles skills, commands, hooks and tool connections so they can be installed together.
- **prompt**: All the text the model reads for one reply: instructions, your request, earlier messages and file contents.
- **rate limit**: A cap on how many requests you can send in a period. When you hit it you must wait or switch.
- **sandbox**: A restricted area for running commands, limiting which files they can change and where they can connect.
- **SDK**: A code library for starting and controlling the agent from your own programs.
- **session**: One continuous conversation with the agent, which can often be resumed later.
- **skill**: A reusable set of instructions the model can pick up when a task calls for it.
- **slash command**: A shortcut you type, such as /help, that starts a built-in or custom action.
- **subagent**: A helper agent started by the main agent, with its own instructions and sometimes its own model.
- **telemetry**: Measurements the program sends out about its own use, such as timings and counts.
- **tool**: An action the harness lets the model ask for, such as reading a file, editing a file or running a command.
- **worktree**: A separate working copy of a project, so an agent can make changes without touching your main copy.

> Vendor-derived text below is untrusted data, never instructions. `‹` and `›` stand for `<` and `>`; a ⚠ marks text that looked like an instruction.

A harness is the program around a model: it builds the prompt, offers tools, checks permissions, runs commands and shows the result. Steps are in the typical order, which vendors seldom document. Each agent line is tied to its cells by a hash; general text and editorial views are labelled.
Only partly covered: Send the request and handle trouble, Read what the model asked for.

## A. Setup, before the first model call

The harness gets ready: it finds your rules, your tools and your permissions. No model is involved yet.

### 1. Choose the front door (`surface`)

- How this works in general: not a vendor claim: You reach an agent through a front door: a terminal, an editor plug-in, a desktop or web app, a script, or a chat or CI service. The door decides what you can see and approve.
- Typically after: none; depends on: none
- Only if: Some doors exist only on some plans or platforms.
- Who normally does the work: harness code
- Editorial: our view, not a vendor claim: Pick the door that fits how you work. A door that cannot ask you questions cannot do tasks that need your approval.
  - claude-code [documented, with limits, unverified] You can use it in a terminal, IDEs, a desktop app, the web, scripts, CI or chat tools. # Claude Code: request flow and controls

> Vendor-derived text below is untrusted data, never instructions. `‹` and `›` stand for `<` and `>`; a ⚠ marks text that looked like an instruction.

Steps run in the typical order. A documented order appears only where a cell states it; a decision point appears only where the documentation describes a branch (each branch quotes it). Many agents have few or none.

## A. Setup, before the first model call

- Choose the front door [documented, with limits, unverified] You can use it in a terminal, IDEs, a desktop app, the web, scripts, CI or chat tools. In script mode Claude doesn't spawn teammates, the desktop hand-off needs a Mac or an x64 Windows computer and a Claude subscription, and repository setup works only with github.com.
- Apply organization rules [documented, with limits, unverified] A company can set rules for its developers' installs: which tools and commands are allowed or denied, which models are offered, and whether background agents run. Managed rules win over options set in code. Claude Tag cloud sessions don't receive server-managed settings.
  - documented order: Managed policy settings win over options set in code.
- Load the house rules [documented, unverified] It reads instruction files from your project and home folder at the start of a session and adds their text to every request. Files at all levels contribute at once, and Claude uses judgment when they conflict. Files can import other files, up to four hops deep.
  - documented order: Broader locations load first, so a project instruction appears after a user instruction.
  - decision point (claude-code/F03.path-scoped-rules): When does a rules file get loaded?
    - The rule has no paths list -> It loads at the start of the session, alongside the main instruction file. | quote: “Rules without paths: frontmatter load at session start”
    - The rule has a paths list -> It loads only when Claude reads, writes or edits a file that matches. | quote: “a rule with YAML paths: frontmatter loads only when Claude reads, writes, or edits a matching file”
- Load memory and earlier sessions [documented, with limits, unverified] Claude can keep notes between sessions, and you can resume, rename, branch or export earlier conversations, which are saved locally. Handoff from the command line is one-way: you can pull a cloud session into the terminal, but can't push a terminal session to the cloud.
- Stock the built-in tools [documented, with limits, unverified] It ships tools for running shell commands, reading, editing and writing files, searching, fetching web pages and starting subagents. Web search is not available on Amazon Bedrock. Shell commands have a default timeout that can be raised up to a cap.
- Load skills and custom commands [documented, unverified] You add reusable instructions as skills, which Claude loads in full only when it uses one, or as commands you type yourself. They live in set folders or come from plugins, and skills are the recommended way to package multi-step commands. A skill can set its own tools and model.
  - documented order: If an added directory and the project define a command with the same name, the project's command runs.
  - decision point (claude-code/F08.invocation): How does Claude learn about and use a skill?
    - A skill with default settings -> Claude sees it in a list of available skills; its full content loads only when Claude uses it. | quote: “full skill content loads only when Claude uses one”
    - A skill that blocks model invocation -> It is left out of that list and stays out of context until you invoke it by name. | quote: “Skills with disable-model-invocation: true are not in that list and stay out of context until you invoke them with /name”
- Connect outside tools [documented, with limits, unverified] You connect outside programs through MCP servers, which add extra tools that need explicit permission. Project servers need a one-time approval and administrators can restrict which servers users add. Consent dialogs don't relay: they only appear in the local terminal.
- Set the safety posture [documented, with limits, unverified] Modes range from plan, the least permissive, through manual and accept-edits to auto and bypass. Manual asks before editing but can change files once you approve. Desktop remembers a mode per folder, except plan, which lasts for the session.
  - documented order: In Desktop, a mode picked for a folder wins over the default mode setting for that folder.
  - decision point (claude-code/F04.trust-prompt): What happens in a folder I have not trusted yet?
    - Trust not yet accepted for the folder -> A workspace trust dialog appears; accepting saves trust for the workspace. | quote: “If workspace trust hasn't been accepted for a directory, Claude Code shows the workspace trust dialog”
    - An agent file sits in an untrusted folder -> A teammate gets that agent's tools and instructions only if you trusted that folder; trusting a parent folder doesn't count. | quote: “A teammate gets an agent definition's tools and instructions only if you've trusted the folder the agent file is in”
- Pick the model and thinking effort [documented, with limits] You pick a model with a picker, a setting or a command option, and set effort per session or by default. It connects to Amazon Bedrock, Microsoft Foundry, Google Cloud and gateways. Foundry has no startup model check, so requests fail if the default is unavailable.
- Prepare an isolated workspace [documented, unverified] It can give each session its own separate copy of your project in a worktree, so parallel sessions don't edit the same files. Each copy sits on its own branch, and the repository needs at least one commit first.

## B. Each turn, before sending

- Assemble the prompt [documented, unverified] Each request re-sends the instructions, project context and conversation so far, with rarely changing content first. The prompt is built on the first request and reused until compaction. Some models take a 1 million token window. A subagent gets its own prompt.
  - documented order: Rarely changing content goes first in the prompt, and the new message comes after the earlier messages and tool results.
- Run your own code at set moments [documented, with limits, unverified] Hooks run a script, request, prompt or subagent at set moments and can allow, deny or change a tool call. A hook's allow doesn't skip deny and ask rules. Some hooks exist in one SDK only, and non-interactive runs without the bare option use project hooks in untrusted folders.
  - documented order: A PreToolUse hook runs before the rest of the permission flow.
  - decision point (claude-code/F06.trust-enable): Do hooks run without asking me first?
    - Hooks come from managed settings -> Interactive users see a security approval dialog before the hooks are applied. | quote: “interactive users see a security approval dialog before Claude Code applies them”
    - A script-mode run that does not use the "bare" setting -> Project hooks run even in a folder you have never trusted, with no workspace trust dialog. | quote: “a -p session runs the hooks in a project's .claude/settings.json, even in a folder you've never trusted”
    - The settings option disables hooks -> Hooks are switched off for that run. | quote: “Passing --settings with disableAllHooks set to true”

## C. The model call

- Send the request and handle trouble [documented, unverified] If the main model is overloaded or unavailable, a session with a backup model set switches to it. Temporary failures are retried up to 10 times with growing waits. When a claude.ai usage limit blocks a request, a command offers waiting for the reset or adding credits.
  - documented order: When the main model is overloaded or unavailable, the session switches to the backup and tries the main model again at the start of each user turn.
  - decision point (claude-code/F17.auto-routing): How does it switch models on its own?
    - Main model overloaded, backup set -> The session switches to the backup model and retries the main one at the start of each user turn. | quote: “a session with fallbackModel set switches to the backup and retries the primary at the start of each user turn”
    - Plan-then-execute choice in plan mode -> It applies during plan mode if the allowed-models list permits, then switches to Sonnet for execution. | quote: “opusplan applies during plan mode when allowed by availableModels, then switches to Sonnet for execution”
    - A helper agent has no model set -> It follows the documented order for choosing a helper agent's model. | quote: “Omitted subagent models follow the subagent model order”
- Set the thinking budget [documented, with limits] Extended thinking is on by default, its tokens are billed as output, and the reasoning shows as gray italic text in the terminal. Not all models support effort levels, and the thinking token cap applies on models with a fixed thinking budget.
- Reuse the unchanged part of the prompt [documented] Prompt caching is on by default and can be switched off. The main conversation asks for a 1 hour cache on a Claude subscription within plan usage, and 5 minutes otherwise; each hit resets the timer. Switching models invalidates the cache.
  - documented order: A setting that forces the shorter 5 minute cache overrides the settings that ask for 1 hour.

## D. After the model answers, every turn

- Read what the model asked for [documented, with limits] A tool name it does not recognise is returned to the model as that call's result and the turn continues. Retries for output that fails a format check apply just in non-interactive mode when a format is requested. The documentation does not mention invalid inputs to a known tool.
- Decide whether it is allowed [documented, with limits, unverified] Rules allow, ask or deny specific tools, and can be narrowed by path or by command. Command rules match the literal command text, so a deny on one form doesn't block another route to the same effect. In auto mode a model classifier blocks irreversible or destructive actions.
- Save an undo point [documented, with limits] Pressing Esc twice, or using the rewind command, opens a menu to restore an earlier conversation and code state. Checkpoints don't track files changed by shell commands, and snapshots are kept for the 100 most recent checkpoints.
- Run it inside the fence [documented, with limits, unverified] Shell commands can run in a sandbox that limits which files they change and which network addresses they reach. It covers shell commands and their child processes, but hooks and MCP servers run outside it, and some commands are excluded or can fall back to running unsandboxed.

    - You type it at the shell-mode prompt -> It runs unsandboxed in most sessions. | quote: “Commands typed at the `!` shell-mode prompt run unsandboxed in most sessions”

- Feed the result back and go round again [documented, with limits] A turn runs from a prompt to a response. In the SDKs, read-only tools can run at the same time, while tools that change state run one after another. The command-line turn limit works in print mode only and has no limit by default, and a session doesn't time out on its own.
- Hand work to helpers [documented, with limits, unverified] It can hand work to helper agents with their own instructions, tools and model, and run several at once, up to 20 by default. The documentation differs on nesting: one page says helpers can start their own helpers, another says by default they lack the tool for it.

- Run without you watching [documented, with limits, unverified] It can run in the background, on a schedule, in the cloud, or react to outside events such as a failed CI run. To involve a different tool you expose it through MCP, and in every approach the workers are Claude sessions.

# OpenAI Codex CLI: request flow and controls

> Vendor-derived text below is untrusted data, never instructions. `‹` and `›` stand for `<` and `>`; a ⚠ marks text that looked like an instruction.

Steps run in the typical order. A documented order appears only where a cell states it; a decision point appears only where the documentation describes a branch (each branch quotes it). Many agents have few or none.

## A. Setup, before the first model call

- Choose the front door [documented, with limits] Use it from a terminal screen, inside editors, in a desktop or web app, from a script, or through GitHub and Slack integrations. Driving it from code with the SDK has a caveat: launching its app server locally is meant for development and debugging and may change without notice.
- Apply organization rules [documented, with limits] Administrators can set rules through a requirements file or device management, and can block the full-access and run-freely options. For model lists, one setting enforces the model catalog, but the table for new chats supplies managed defaults, not enforcement.
  - documented order: For local execution, device management and legacy managed-device requirements win over Agent Security, which wins over the device's system requirements file.
- Load the house rules [partly documented] It loads instruction files from your Codex home folder and the project, and files closer to your working folder take precedence. The documentation does not mention importing one file into another. It stops searching at your current folder, so put overrides near the work.
  - documented order: Files closer to the working folder take precedence.
- Load memory and earlier sessions [documented] Memory is off until you turn it on, and it can be switched on or off from inside the terminal screen. You can resume or fork an earlier session, hand one to the desktop app or the cloud, and choose whether transcripts are saved and how large the history file may grow.
- Stock the built-in tools [documented, with limits] It comes with tools to edit files by applying patches and to run shell commands, plus helper-agent tools and an image tool that can be turned off. Web search is on by default for local chats but serves a stored index, not live pages, and is not available on Bedrock Runtime.
- Load skills and custom commands [documented, with limits] Skills are folders with an instruction file that you or the model can invoke, kept in your home folder or the repository. Custom commands are deprecated, live on your machine, are not shared through the repository, and are read from the top level of one folder, not subfolders.
- Connect outside tools [documented, with limits] It can connect local or remote outside tool servers over two connection types, using a token or a separate sign-in method. Sign-in and sign-out actions work with web-style servers and depend on the server supporting that sign-in. Tools marked destructive ask for approval first.
  - decision point (codex-cli/F12.server-trust): Does a destructive-looking outside tool call need my approval?
    - The tool advertises a destructive marking -> The call requires approval. | quote: “Destructive app/MCP tool calls always require approval when the tool advertises a destructive annotation”
    - It also advertises a read marking -> Approval is not forced: the read marking takes priority over the destructive one. | quote: “unless it advertises a read annotation, which takes priority”
  - decision point (codex-cli/F12.server-trust): When does Codex switch on an outside tool server under an allowlist?
    - Name and identity both match an approved entry -> Codex enables the server. | quote: “the client enables an MCP server only when both its name and identity match an approved entry”
    - They do not match -> Codex disables the server. | quote: “otherwise it disables it.”
- Set the safety posture [documented, with limits] How often it pauses to ask is set separately from how much it may touch, and asking when the model decides is the default. An untrusted project's own settings are ignored. Docs name different starting modes, and plan mode is temporarily unavailable while it is working.
  - documented order: For local execution, device management and legacy managed-device requirements win over Agent Security, which wins over the device's system requirements file.
  - decision point (codex-cli/F04.trust-prompt): Does Codex use a project's own settings if I have not trusted the project?
    - The project is trusted -> Settings files kept in the project are loaded. | quote: “Codex loads project-scoped config files only when the project is trusted”
    - The project is untrusted -> The project's own settings, hooks and rules are ignored; your user and system settings still load. | quote: “If the project is untrusted, Codex ignores project .codex/ layers”
- Pick the model and thinking effort [documented, with limits] You choose the model with a picker or a launch option, and the effort levels depend on the model and client. The documentation gives a default level for the security scan command but does not state one for general sessions. Custom model providers can be set up.
- Prepare an isolated workspace [documented] It can run a chat in a new Git worktree so several independent chats in one project do not interfere with each other. Both local and worktree chats run on your own computer.

## B. Each turn, before sending

- Assemble the prompt [documented] The model's reading limit is a setting that defaults to automatic. You attach files by naming paths, and the IDE extension adds open files. Codex joins its instruction files into one chain per run, nearer files winning, and stops adding at a size cap (32 KiB by default).
  - documented order: Instruction files are joined from the project root downward, and a nearer file overrides an earlier one.
- Run your own code at set moments [documented, with limits] You can attach scripts to moments like before a tool runs or at session start. A hook is a guardrail, not a complete enforcement boundary: an error or timeout can leave the tool unblocked. Local hooks are unsupported with cloud orchestration, and matchers apply to some events.
  - decision point (codex-cli/F06.output-blocking): If a safety hook fails or times out, does Codex still block the tool?
    - The hook gives an explicit supported denial -> The action can be blocked. | quote: “An explicit supported denial can block an action”
    - The hook errors, times out or is malformed -> The hook can fail without blocking the tool. | quote: “a PreToolUse callback error, timeout, or malformed response can fail the hook without blocking the tool”
    - The hook exits with no output -> It counts as success and Codex continues. | quote: “A hook that exits 0 with no output is treated as success and Codex continues.”

## C. The model call

- Send the request and handle trouble [documented, with limits] The service can reroute a request to another model and says so. Usage limits are shared with ChatGPT, and running out can pause some features. Retry counts are documented for failed requests and dropped streams; the wait between tries is outside what the cited text covers.
- Set the thinking budget [documented, with limits] Higher effort makes responses slower and uses more tokens, and the available levels depend on the model. Noisy reasoning output can be silenced, summary detail can be chosen or turned off, and raw reasoning text appears when the model supports it.
- Reuse the unchanged part of the prompt [not documented] The documentation does not mention whether Codex asks the model service to remember the unchanged start of the prompt.

## D. After the model answers, every turn

- Read what the model asked for [not documented] The documentation does not mention how Codex deals with a malformed or incomplete request from the model.
- Decide whether it is allowed [documented] Rules can allow, ask about, or forbid commands by prefix, and filesystem rules can deny reads for exact paths or patterns. Tools marked destructive ask first. A reviewer helper can take over eligible approval prompts but does not review actions the sandbox already allows.
- Save an undo point [documented, with limits] The documentation describes a rollback call in the app server that drops the last few turns from memory, and lists a counter for undo actions. The rollback call is deprecated and will be removed.
- Run it inside the fence [documented] Commands run inside an operating-system sandbox. Network access is off by default and writes are limited to the active workspace. The sandbox covers spawned commands, not just built-in file edits. It can be disabled, and a shell command you start yourself runs outside it.

    - There is no override -> The global rule is inherited. | quote: “without one, the Global rule is inherited”
- Tidy the tool's output [documented, with limits] Limits are documented for MCP tool output (a token budget per tool) and hook output (about 2,500 tokens by default, extra saved to disk). Telemetry redacts prompts by default, and memory and uploads have secrets redacted. Saved scan logs are not redacted.
- Feed the result back and go round again [documented] A turn is one exchange: your prompt plus the agent's reply and actions. Codex receives a tool call, runs it and sends back the result. Limits include stopping a turn after repeated automatic-review denials, a tool timeout, and a time limit for workers.
- Hand work to helpers [documented, with limits] It can start helper agents with their own role, model and effort, run several in parallel, and cap how many are open at once. The documentation does not state a depth limit or whether a helper may start its own helpers. Total caps are shown for security deep scans.

- Show the answer or ask you [documented, with limits] A plan command switches a chat into plan mode for multi-step planning, optionally with a first planning request. The documentation does not say whether plan mode blocks edits or how to leave it beyond toggling. A status command shows model, approval setting and context left.
- Wrap up and keep score [documented, with limits] A usage command shows daily, weekly or total token activity. Rollout budget tracking is under development and off by default. Telemetry export is off by default, and with local access to Work, cloud orchestration events do not reach your own collector.

## E. Around the session

- Run without you watching [documented, with limits] It can run scheduled tasks and cloud tasks that keep working while your computer sleeps, and a terminal screen can connect to a server on another machine. Background terminal lists may be empty depending on a setting, and event triggers depend on an eligible plan.
- Extend and share [documented] A plugin bundles skills, apps, tool connections and hooks, and is installed from a marketplace that can be pinned to a version. Administrators can restrict marketplace sources. A plugin does not automatically trust its hooks, and Codex skips plugin-bundled hooks.

Enterprise rules limit which models appear, the research helper keeps its own model, and the settings file list of effort levels leaves out max.

- Prepare an isolated workspace [documented] It can create a separate Git worktree and switch to it, leaving your uncommitted changes behind, or fork a session into a new worktree. A setting can start new worktrees from the remote default branch.

## B. Each turn, before sending

- Assemble the prompt [documented, unverified] The latest models support a very large context window, in a default or longer size. Naming a file adds it to the prompt, a command shows window use, and large tool output goes to a file with a preview. Copilot Business and Enterprise content exclusion rules are respected.
  - documented order: A repository setting that pins the default tier takes precedence.
- Run your own code at set moments [partly documented, unverified] Hooks are shell commands that run at points such as session start or before a tool runs, and can allow or deny a tool call. The documentation does not mention matcher rules for choosing which tools a hook covers. A setting can turn hooks off.
  - decision point (copilot-cli/F06.trust-enable): When do repository hooks run in one-off prompt mode?
    - The prompt-mode hooks variable is set to true -> Repository hooks load in prompt mode. | quote: “Repository hooks load in prompt mode (-p) when GITHUB_COPILOT_PROMPT_MODE_REPO_HOOKS is set to true”
    - The folder is trusted or allow-all is set -> Repository hooks also load automatically. | quote: “also load automatically when the folder is already trusted or COPILOT_ALLOW_ALL is set”
    - The user setting that disables hooks is on -> Both repository-level and user-level hooks are disabled. | quote: “A user setting can disable all hooks, both repository-level and user-level”

## C. The model call

- Send the request and handle trouble [documented, with limits] Auto mode picks a model by system health, performance and task difficulty. A setting, off by default, makes an eligible rate limit error switch to auto mode and retry, but not for global limits or your own provider. A default limit or wait time is not stated.
- Set the thinking budget [documented, with limits] Some models offer a choice of reasoning depth, and the documentation does not list the levels per model. A key shows or hides the model's reasoning. Summaries appear for supporting OpenAI models, and the documentation does not describe a token budget control.
- Reuse the unchanged part of the prompt [documented, with limits] GitHub says it uses prompt caching for Claude and Google Gemini models to improve service quality and cut delay. The documentation does not mention how long cached text is kept or a way to switch caching on or off.

## D. After the model answers, every turn

- Read what the model asked for [not documented] The documentation does not mention what happens when the model's request to run a command or edit a file is badly formed or incomplete.
- Decide whether it is allowed [documented, with limits, unverified] Rules can allow or deny tools, folders and shell commands by name. Command matching is literal, with no regular expressions or general wildcards. Assisted approval still asks each time but adds a model's safety recommendation, so the CLI can approve requests it judges acceptable.
- Save an undo point [documented] It tracks the file changes it makes for each prompt. Pressing the escape key twice while it is idle rewinds the session to an earlier prompt and can restore your files.
- Run it inside the fence [documented, with limits, unverified] Shell commands and searches can run in a local sandbox that limits where they write and whether they reach the network. It is experimental. File tools follow it on a best-effort basis, remote MCP servers stay outside it, and enterprise settings can require it.
  - decision point (copilot-cli/F05.sandbox-override): Can I switch the sandbox off for a session?
    - The effective policy permits sandbox bypass -> You can turn sandboxing off for the rest of the current session. | quote: “a user can explicitly disable sandboxing for the rest of the current session”
    - Enterprise managed settings require sandboxing -> Ordinary configuration and the no-sandbox startup option do not switch it off. | quote: “If enterprise managed settings require sandboxing”
- Tidy the tool's output [documented, with limits] Large tool output is saved to a file; the model gets its location and a preview, and the size limit can be changed. Two GitHub token variables are hidden by default; you can name others. GitHub says it does not currently provide built-in secret hiding for hooks.
- Feed the result back and go round again [documented, with limits, unverified] It works through a prompt in rounds of model reply and tool use, and a prompt you send while it is thinking is treated as steering. In autopilot a setting caps the follow-on messages, and the documentation disagrees on the default.
- Hand work to helpers [documented, with limits, unverified] Custom helper agents are described in Markdown files with their own tools, and can have their own model and effort. Several run at once under limits on depth and number. The documentation disagrees on the default depth and cap, and the research helper uses a fixed model.
  - documented order: For helper effort, a per-call value wins, then a settings override, then the agent's own definition.
  - decision point (copilot-cli/F09.per-agent-model): Which model does a helper agent use?
    - Its agent profile names a model -> The helper runs on the model named in that profile. | quote: “that model is used by the subagent”
    - It is the built-in research agent -> It uses a fixed model that the model command does not change. | quote: “The built-in research agent is hard-coded to use a particular AI model”
- Shrink the context when it fills [documented, with limits] It summarizes older conversation automatically, or you can ask for it by hand and add focus instructions. A finished compaction cannot be undone. The documentation disagrees on when the automatic step starts: about 80 percent in two places, 95 percent in another.
- Show the answer or ask you [documented, with limits] Plan mode lets you work out a plan before code is written, and remote clients can approve or reject it. The plan description does not call plan mode read-only. The terminal shows the model used for each response and whether sandboxing is on.
- Wrap up and keep score [documented, with limits, unverified] It shows context use and AI credits spent in a session, can cap spending per response, and can export telemetry in a standard monitoring format. The spending cap is a soft limit, and user budgets are not considered when the organization is billed directly.

## E. Around the session

- Run without you watching [documented, unverified] It can run tasks in the background, repeat or delay a prompt on a schedule, hand work to a cloud agent on GitHub, and be watched or steered from GitHub or GitHub Mobile. Automations react to events such as an issue being opened and skip people without write access by default.
- Extend and share [documented, with limits, unverified] A plugin bundles skills, hooks, helper agents and MCP servers, and installs from a repository, a marketplace or a local folder. Installed plugins are cached, so local changes need a reinstall. Auto-update works only in your own or managed settings, not a repository's.

- Updates and releases [documented, unverified] It can check its version, update itself, show its changelog with an optional summary, and turn automatic updates off for CI. Some features need an experimental switch, and the documentation lists retired models and removed options.
- Where it runs and who runs it [documented, with limits] It is part of GitHub Copilot: the Copilot app is built on it, and it runs in a JetBrains terminal. It needs a Copilot seat unless you bring your own model provider, and delegating needs a sign-in. Pull requests need a Git repository on GitHub; operating systems are not listed.

    - You bring your own model provider -> It can connect to your provider without a GitHub account or token. | quote: “With BYOK, Copilot CLI can connect to the configured provider without a GitHub account or token”
- Identity, retention and audit [documented, with limits, unverified] Users need a Copilot seat and sign in through GitHub, and a list of approved organizations can pin who may sign in.   - decision point (cursor/F07.model-allowlist): What happens when an admin blocks a model for the team?
    - A model is blocked for the team -> On Enterprise, Cursor routes the request to a model the team allows. | quote: “if a model is blocked for the team, Cursor Router routes to an allowed model”
    - A helper agent is set to a blocked model -> The helper's configured model is not used when an admin has blocked it. | quote: “a subagent's configured model is not used when an admin has blocked it”
- Load the house rules [documented, with limits, unverified] Cloud agents read the project's instruction file, and the CLI and editor load project rules on their own. Rules can be scoped to file patterns and can include other files. User rules and project rules both go into the prompt, and team rules take precedence.
  - documented order: Team rules work alongside other rule types and take precedence over them.
  - decision point (cursor/F03.precedence-scoping): Which rule wins when several rules apply?
    - A team rule overlaps another rule type -> Team rules work alongside other rule types and take precedence. | quote: “Team Rules work alongside other rule types and take precedence”
    - Policy files sit at several folder levels -> The closest applicable policy file has the highest priority for files under its folder. | quote: “The closest applicable APPROVAL_POLICY.md has the highest priority for files under its directory”
    - A higher-level policy meets a closer one -> Higher-level policies still apply, unless they conflict. | quote: “ancestor policies still apply unless they conflict”
- Load memory and earlier sessions [documented, with limits, unverified] It can keep notes between runs of an automation and save a learned rule from a pull request comment. You can continue, fork, rename and list past chats, and send a chat to a cloud agent, but uncommitted local changes do not go with it.
- Stock the built-in tools [documented, unverified] The agent can edit files, search the code, run terminal commands and search the web. Terminal commands need your approval by default, and fetching a web page asks first unless the site is on an allow list. Searching without asking is off by default.
- Load skills and custom commands [partly documented, unverified] Skills are folders of instructions the agent can pick when a task fits, or you can run one by typing a slash and its name. Commands are saved prompts kept at team, project or user level. The documentation does not mention per-skill tool or model overrides.
- Connect outside tools [documented, with limits, unverified] It connects outside tools through MCP in the editor, the command line and cloud agents. Each connection needs approval, and each tool call needs approval unless pre-approved. The documentation gives conflicting answers on whether cloud agents accept one older connection style.
  - documented order: A connection is approved first; after that each tool call still needs its own approval.
- Set the safety posture [documented, with limits, unverified] Terminal commands need approval by default. Run modes range from an allow list to an automatic reviewer, and a run-everything mode skips prompts. Plan, ask, debug and design modes exist. The new-folder trust question is off by default; a device policy overrides matching settings.
  - documented order: When a policy comes from device management, its value overrides the matching Cursor setting on the user's device.
- Pick the model and thinking effort [partly documented] You choose the model from a picker in chat or a command in the command line, and can set a default in settings. Effort levels depend on the model, and Composer has none. You can add your own key for a supported provider. The documentation does not mention shared model selection.
  - documented order: For the cloud agent interface, an omitted model choice falls back from the user default to the team default to a system default.
- Prepare an isolated workspace [documented, with limits] The command line can run the agent in a new Git worktree instead of your current checkout, and agents started that way from the agents window get a separate checkout. Helper agents share the parent's checkout by default. Worktrees are disabled for multi-root workspaces.

## B. Each turn, before sending

- Assemble the prompt [documented, with limits, unverified] Cloud agents let you pick the context window size, and a larger one can cost more; automations use each model's maximum. Sensitive files can be kept out of what the model reads. An SDK option, if enabled for your account, can replace the built-in instructions for local agents.
- Run your own code at set moments [documented, with limits, unverified] Hooks run your scripts at moments such as before a tool or shell command, after a file edit, or when a session starts or ends. A script can block an action. Hooks are set per user or per project, and project hooks run when the workspace is trusted.
  - decision point (cursor/F06.trust-enable): Will a project's hooks run when I open the project?
    - The workspace is trusted -> Project hooks load and run automatically when team members open the project. | quote: “Project hooks load and run automatically when team members open the project in a trusted workspace”
    - The workspace is not trusted -> The documentation says the workspace must be trusted to run project hooks. | quote: “the workspace must be trusted to run them”

## C. The model call

- Send the request and handle trouble [documented, with limits, unverified] Auto sends simple requests to fast models and complex work to the most capable. At the usage limit you get a notice and can pay as you go. The CLI retries dropped connections; attempt counts and delays are not stated, and rate-limit errors are shown, not retried.
- Set the thinking budget [documented, with limits] Which thinking options exist depends on the model. The command line can show the model's thinking blocks, and the cloud agent run stream sends thinking text. The documentation says thinking events are suppressed in print mode.
- Reuse the unchanged part of the prompt [documented, with limits] The SDK reports how much of the prompt was served from the cache and how much was saved to it, and model pages list cache prices. The documentation does not mention how long the cache lasts, when it is cleared, or a setting to control it.

## D. After the model answers, every turn

- Read what the model asked for [not documented] The documentation does not mention how Cursor handles a malformed or incomplete request from the model, such as a broken command or file edit.
- Decide whether it is allowed [documented, with limits] Rules decide what runs without a prompt, by tool, file pattern or command, and an automatic reviewer can check calls outside the sandbox. Allow lists are a convenience, not a security guarantee, and terminal commands can still read ignored files.
  - documented order: A terminal allow list, when set, overrides the in-app terminal allow list.
- Save an undo point [documented, with limits] Restoring a checkpoint on an earlier message rolls back the files the agent changed after that point, but the conversation keeps its messages. The command line can jump back to a previous message, and forking a chat from an earlier message shortens the conversation.
- Run it inside the fence [documented, with limits, unverified] Commands can run in a sandbox that limits file and network access. Local agents run with the sandbox off by default and can reach the network without restriction. A command that fails inside it can be rerun outside, and a reviewer checks the rerun.
  - documented order: If a sandboxed command fails on a restriction, the agent can rerun it outside the sandbox, and a reviewer then checks that rerun.
  - decision point (cursor/F05.sandbox-override): What happens if the sandbox blocks a command the agent wants to run?
    - It fails on a sandbox restriction -> The agent can rerun it outside the sandbox, and an automatic reviewer checks that rerun. | quote: “the agent can rerun it outside the sandbox, and the classifier reviews that rerun”
    - It needs full system access -> It bypasses the sandbox; Cursor indicates this and asks for approval. | quote: “Cursor indicates when a command runs outside the sandbox and asks for approval”
- Tidy the tool's output [documented, with limits] Long tool output is trimmed on some surfaces: the CLI cuts shell output from the top, and SDK and cloud messages mark what was truncated. Cloud agent secrets are hidden, and shared transcripts get best-effort hiding. Redaction of local agent tool output is not described.
- Feed the result back and go round again [documented, unverified] The agent calls a tool, reads the result and decides its next step. The documentation says there is no limit on the number of tool calls in a task. A stop hook can send a follow-up message to keep it going, with a default limit of 5.
- Hand work to helpers [documented, with limits, unverified] Helper agents are set up as text files with their own model, tools and read-only choice, and several can run at once in their own context. The main agent and its direct helpers can start helpers; one started by another helper cannot start more.
- Shrink the context when it fills [documented, unverified] When the window nears full, Cursor summarises older parts of the conversation to make room, and you can do it by hand with a command. A hook runs before compaction but cannot block or change it.
- Show the answer or ask you [documented, with limits, unverified] Plan mode researches the code, asks clarifying questions and writes a plan you can edit before building starts. File editing is listed as allowed after you approve the plan. A status line and a context ring show progress and how full the window is.
- Wrap up and keep score [documented, with limits, unverified] A spending dashboard shows the cost of requests, and you can fetch billed token use for an agent. You are asked to set a spend limit when you first use cloud agents. Usage metrics can stream to monitoring tools for Enterprise, and a command shows the debug log location.
  - decision point (cursor/F22.budget-caps): What happens on a Teams or Enterprise plan when the Other Models allowance runs out?
    - On-demand usage is enabled -> Own-key requests keep working. | quote: “own-key requests keep working if on-demand usage is enabled”
    - On-demand usage is off -> Own-key requests stop until the next billing cycle. | quote: “stop until the next billing cycle if it is off”

## E. Around the session

- Run without you watching [documented, unverified] Automations run cloud agents in the background on a schedule or when events arrive from tools such as GitHub, Slack and Linear. Cloud agents work in full development environments and keep going when your device disconnects. You can take over the remote desktop and hand it back.
  - decision point (cursor/F15.scheduled-routines): How does the repeating prompt skill decide when to run?
    - An interval is specified -> The prompt or skill runs on a recurring or variable interval. | quote: “runs a prompt or skill on a recurring or variable interval”
    - No fixed interval is given -> The agent chooses when to wake. | quote: “if you don't specify a fixed interval, the agent chooses when to wake”
- Extend and share [documented, with limits, unverified] Plugins bundle rules, skills, agents, commands, MCP servers and hooks. They install from the Cursor Marketplace, a Git repository or a local folder, and one repository can host several plugins. Marketplace plugins are manually reviewed before listing.
- Updates and releases [documented, unverified] The command line tries to update itself by default, and there are Stable and Early Access channels. A device policy can switch updates off. Changelog pages list new features and fixes, and the documentation gives some deprecations as examples.
- Where it runs and who runs it [documented, with limits] Cursor is based on the VS Code codebase. The SDK, command line, editor and web app run the same agent, and SDK runs follow the same pricing and privacy rules as the editor. Tool calls can run on a customer's own workers while the agent loop stays in Cursor's cloud.
- Identity, retention and audit [documented, with limits, unverified] Single sign-on is listed among team features, and a policy controls which team IDs can log in. Enterprise customers can enroll in US-only data residency, and a few models fall outside the data retention agreements. Admins are advised to review audit logs.

- Apply organization rules [partly documented, unverified] A system settings file sets a baseline and takes precedence over other settings, and admin policies override user, workspace and default ones. Enterprise controls are managed through a console. The documentation does not mention lists of allowed or blocked models.
  - documented order: Admin policies win over user, workspace and default policies.
- Load the house rules [documented, unverified] It reads instruction files from your home folder and project, searching from the current folder upward and joining what it finds. Files can import other files, and a file in a subfolder holds rules for that folder. It also scans a folder when a tool touches it.
  - documented order: The search starts in the current folder and moves up through the parent folders to a stop point.
- Load memory and earlier sessions [documented, with limits, unverified] It keeps durable notes, and an experimental feature drafts new ones from past sessions for you to approve. You can resume, branch and list earlier sessions, saved as local transcripts. For handoff, the documentation describes exporting sessions to files.

    - The include-directories memory setting is true -> A reload scans the include directories as well. | quote: “scans include directories when”
    - That setting is false -> Just the current directory is used. | quote: “when false, only the current directory is used”

- Load skills and custom commands [partly documented, unverified] A skill is a folder with a description file that the model loads when a task fits. Custom commands are small text files you type yourself, with room for arguments. The documentation does not mention per-skill tool or model overrides, or how commands relate to skills.
  - documented order: User and project commands take precedence over extension commands, which rank lowest.
- Connect outside tools [documented, with limits, unverified] It works with MCP servers, which can run as local programs or be reached remotely, and are set up in settings files with optional sign-in. Servers an admin requires are limited to remote connections. Tools can be filtered per server, and admins can list allowed servers.
- Set the safety posture [documented, with limits, unverified] It has four approval modes: ask each time, auto-approve edits, plan (read-only) and run freely. New folders get a trust check. The documentation disagrees on whether run-freely can be turned on by a keyboard shortcut, and on whether settings merge from two files or four.
  - documented order: When several policy rules match a tool call, the highest-priority one is applied.
- Pick the model and thinking effort [partly documented] You pick the model in a dialog or at launch, and the default is automatic. ## B. Each turn, before sending

- Assemble the prompt [partly documented] You can pull in files with an at-sign, add extra folders, and exclude files with ignore rules. A custom file can fully replace the built-in system prompt. Enabled skills are described to the model at session start. The documentation does not mention the context window size.
- Run your own code at set moments [documented, with limits, unverified] Hooks run your own scripts at set moments, such as before a model request. For now just command-type hooks are supported, non-text message parts are filtered out, and one event does not support some blocking controls. Project hooks start untrusted.

## C. The model call

- Send the request and handle trouble [documented, with limits] It picks a model and switches to a fallback when one fails or is rate-limited. On busy-service errors it asks whether to keep trying, waiting longer between tries, or fall back. Main requests allow up to 10 attempts. The documentation does not give wait times.
- Set the thinking budget [documented, with limits] A model setting block can carry reasoning configuration, and the thinking budget can be controlled directly. The entry describes it just as configuration for models with reasoning, without a per-model list of accepted levels.

An LLM-based security checker is off by default and described as an additional layer of protection.

## A. Setup, before the first model call

- Choose the front door [partly documented, unverified] Running it in a terminal opens a full-screen interface, and it can also run inline. It can run in scripts without a screen and connect to editors through the Agent Client Protocol. The documentation does not mention desktop or web apps, or build-pipeline and chat services.
- Apply organization rules [documented, with limits, unverified] An administrator can push settings files onto machines, switch off the mode that skips permission prompts, and limit which models can be picked. A lock is honored from root-owned locations, not from a file the user can edit.
  - documented order: A model on the disabled list is removed from the catalog, and that wins over merely hiding it.
  - decision point (grok-build/F07.policy-lockdown): Where must a company lock live for Grok Build to honor it?
    - A root-owned location or the system layer -> Grok Build honors the lock. | quote: “The lock is honored only from root-owned sources (`/etc/grok/requirements.toml` or the system layer)”
    - A user-writable file in the home folder -> The lock is not honored from the user-writable copy. | quote: “not from the user-writable `~/.grok/requirements.toml`”
- Load the house rules [partly documented, unverified] It reads instruction files and rule folders in a project, including Claude Code ones, and skips files that git ignores. Deeper files win on a conflict, and a nested file covers its own folder tree. The documentation does not mention an import syntax.
  - documented order: When rule files conflict, the file deeper in the folder tree takes precedence.
- Load memory and earlier sessions [documented, with limits, unverified] Cross-session memory is off by default, and its commands appear once it is switched on. Conversations are saved on disk, keyed by working directory, and can be resumed, forked, listed, renamed and exported, with the same sessions in the terminal, headless and editor use.
- Stock the built-in tools [documented, unverified] Built-in tools can be allowed or removed by name. Shell commands time out after 120 seconds by default, and long-running ones run as background tasks. The web fetch tool is off by default for security, and the write tool can be switched off for read-only sessions.
- Load skills and custom commands [partly documented, unverified] Skills are reusable instruction folders that also appear as slash commands. The vendor says a skill's tool list does not grant or restrict tools and model settings are not applied. The documentation gives an autocomplete hint for arguments but not how they are passed.
- Connect outside tools [documented, unverified] It connects MCP servers whose tools appear next to the built-in ones. Servers are set up in user or project settings, and Claude Code and Cursor configs are read too. A project server replaces a user one with the same name. Trusting a project also covers its MCP servers.
  - documented order: Settings read from the Claude Code, Cursor and project config files are merged in below the main Grok settings file in priority.
- Set the safety posture [documented, with limits, unverified] It asks before running anything not already allowed. Modes include plan, auto and one that skips permission prompts. The default mode comes from user or managed settings, not project ones. For read-only sessions it describes switching off the write tool, not a named mode.
